title: Avail test runner underuses concurrent fibers (200-300% CPU on 12 cores)
description:
Running all the Avail-language tests repeatedly keeps only 2-3 cores busy,
at 200-300% CPU, on a 12-core machine.  This happens with "Run all tests
repeatedly" or "Time all tests_times" in Avail Tests.avail.  The Avail
unit-testing framework forks fibers to run tests concurrently, but far
fewer run at once than Mark expects.  Find out why, and fix it.  (JUnit's
own parallelism, the Gradle side, is a separate matter.)

How the runner schedules tests today (Avail.avail/Unit Testing.avail/
Runners.avail, "recursively report on all tests in_"):
- "recursively visit_,on entering do_,on leaving do_" walks the suite tree
  depth first, one suite at a time, using For each over child suite IDs.
- Within one suite, the tests that have no per-test fixtures run with
  "map parallel in parallel through computeMetric".  The tests that do have
  fixtures, and every test in a suite marked "Do not run tests in_in
  parallel" (file iterator and file access rights tests, for example), then
  run one at a time.
- So concurrency is limited to one suite's parallel tests at a time.  Each
  suite waits for its slowest test, and its serial tests, before the next
  suite starts.  Small suites, or suites with one long test, leave the cores
  idle.  This is the leading hypothesis, but it is not yet measured.

Questions to answer:
- Measure it: how many fibers are runnable over time, and how busy the
  AvailRuntime pool's workers are.  The pool size depends on the processor
  count.  A JFR recording, thread dumps, or fiber counts taken during a
  loop would show this.
- How is "map_in parallel through_" implemented (one fiber per element, or
  bounded)?  Does it add overhead or a limit of its own?
- Apart from the suite structure, do the tests serialize on something else:
  shared variables or locks in the framework (Framework State.avail), the
  L2 optimizer or JVM translation (chunk compilation, nameCounters), or
  output to standard out?
- Would running whole suites concurrently, honoring fixture and
  "do not run in parallel" constraints, raise utilization?  Suite fixture
  setup and teardown must still bracket each suite's tests.

Done when the bottleneck is identified with evidence, and the runner's
scheduling (or whatever else limits it) is changed, so that a full test run
keeps the cores busy, or the limit is explained.
notes: Ruling (Mark, 2026-11-07): a child suite's tests follow the per-test fixture rules they inherit.  So a suite that declares its own per-test fixture (Before running each test in_, or Do not run tests in_in parallel) runs its whole subtree in one sequential chain, as the runner does today.  Child suites' suite-level setup and teardown still bracket their own tests within that chain.  Elsewhere the scheme is concurrent: a suite's setup runs first; then its fixture-free tests, each of its child suites, and its chain of tests that must run one at a time all run concurrently; then its teardown.  Unwrap worker exceptions so that test-fixture-setup and test-fixture-tear-down exceptions keep their types.  Measure CPU use and wall time with Time all tests_times before and after.

title: L2_INVOKE_WITH_OUTERS: call closed code without building the closure
description:
The pattern r1 = L2_CLOSE(code, outers...); L2_INVOKE(r1, args...) is
common.  Replace it with L2_INVOKE_WITH_OUTERS(code, [outers], [args]),
passing outers and arguments together on an interpreter-held argument stack
(extending argsBuffer), callee-pops (or caller-pops, to allow combining
pops), cleared on reification.  A plain L2_INVOKE of a passed-in function
pushes the outers of that function itself.  The full proposal is in this
bead's design field.
design:
Full text of the former avail/doc/Optimization/Level_Two/Function_call_with_outers.md, moved here from doc/ on 2026-11-12 because it is a proposal, not a description of the system:

This pattern occurs a lot in the Avail L2 code:
```
    r1 = L2_CLOSE(code, outer1, outer2, ...)
    L2_INVOKE(r1, arg1, ...)
```

In this situation, we can avoid creating the closure by rewriting it to use a new proposed instruction:

```
L2_INVOKE_WITH_OUTERS(code, [outer1, outer2, ...], [arg1, arg2...])
```

We can alter the calling convention for this.  The interpreter currently has an argsBuffer list to hold just the current call's arguments, but we can extend that to include both outers and arguments, and *not* empty it during calls.  When you do a call, you'd push the outers then the arguments, say in reverse order to make indexing easier.  On exit, the callee clears that number of entries (outers + arguments) from the stack.  On reification, the callee also clears those entries, since the code had to move those values into a continuation anyhow.

So `L2_INVOKE_WITH_OUTERS` would push the outers in reverse, then the arguments in reverse.  The Nth argument would be argStack[argStack.size - N], and an A-argument function would have its Oth outer at argStack[argStack.size - A - O].  Since the call stack cannot exceed something like 50 levels (at which point reification is forced), the argStack will likewise not grow too big.  And we can verify that it's empty after clearing the JVM stack.  When we move to a Rust / native implementation of the VM, we'll just allocate 50xN slots in raw memory, and do heap-allocated stuff for the very rare functions that take more than N arguments+outers.  No bounds checks needed.  And we could allocate downward to make the indexing obvious.

A regular `L2_INVOKE` (say, of a function that is passed in rather than closed within the current graph) would simply extract the function's outers into the stack.  The callee still cleans them up.  That cost is proportional to the number of outers, but a function that closes a lot of outers is probably accessing most of them anyhow, so the extra cost won't be noticed.  And in theory we can optimize the pushes and pops for cases where the same function is invoked multiple times (e.g., for iteration) if there was no other stack access between the calls.  Making it be caller-pops instead of callee-pops would make that simpler, and allow combining pops, or leaving values pushed on the stack that will be needed later.  The callee doesn't care what's below the args+outers that are visible to it.

title: Variant consistency between manifest and restrictions
description:
Step 8 of the manifest redesign (Manifest_ValueClass_Redesign.md): keep the
variant sets in TypeRestriction (they are read where no manifest exists:
L2_GET_OBJECT_FIELD.translateToJVM, L2_GET_OBJECT_TYPE_FIELD,
L2_EXTRACT_OBJECT_VARIANT_ID, and the dispatch lookup trees).  Make the
manifest the sole writer of variant information into restrictions, reconcile
the two at every update, and have L2ValueManifest.check() assert consistency.
No such assertion exists today.
notes:
Text of the former Manifest_ValueClass_Redesign.md "Step 8 — variant consistency", preserved here when the doc was rewritten normatively as doc/Optimization/Level_Two/Value_manifest.md (2026-11-11).  The current doc states only that restrictions carry variant sets because JVM translation and lookup trees read them (§Restrictions):

### Step 8 — variant consistency

Keep the variant sets in `TypeRestriction`. They are **not** redundant: they
are read where no manifest exists — `L2_GET_OBJECT_FIELD.translateToJVM`
chooses `fieldAtIndex` versus `fieldAt` from them, as do
`L2_GET_OBJECT_TYPE_FIELD` and `L2_EXTRACT_OBJECT_VARIANT_ID`; and the
`dispatch/` lookup trees (`InternalLookupTree`,
`ObjectLayoutVariantDecisionStep`, `ObjectTypeLayoutVariantDecisionStep`) are
built and cached per method from bare restrictions, entirely outside L2
generation. JVM translation runs long after manifests are gone.

The manifest's `VariantId(x)` class is the *inference* carrier; the
restriction's variant sets are the *durable* carrier. What can be deleted is
the ad hoc reconstruction in `propagateForRestrictionChange` that converts a
narrowed variant-id range back into `intersectionWithObjectVariant`. Replace
it with an invariant: the manifest is the sole writer of variant information
into restrictions, the two are reconciled at every update, and `check()`
asserts consistency.

title: Dependency graph of postponed instructions (canCommuteWith)
description:
L2Instruction.canCommuteWith (with the ReadsHiddenVariable / WritesHiddenVariable annotations it consults) is unused.  Its KDoc sketches a further design: postponement records, on each edge, a directed graph of postponed instructions whose edges say which must run before which, so instruction scheduling can produce values at the most convenient time around calls, and phi-equivalent instructions can be pulled down through control-flow merges rather than only identical ones.

Decide whether to build that, or to retire canCommuteWith.  Either way, remove the dated "As of 2024.03.13" and "Eventually" plan language from its KDoc: the KDoc should describe what the function does, and this bead carries the plan.

title: E-graph saturation for primitive-invocation equivalences
description:
Listed as out of scope in Manifest_ValueClass_Redesign.md: equivalences of
L2SemanticPrimitiveInvocation driven by declared theorems with a cost model
for extraction (a+a+a to a*3 unless a+a is already computed; {a,a,a} = {a};
|{a,a,a}| = 1).  ValueClass is the e-class and ValueState the e-class data; it
needs a signature table Map<Pair<Primitive, List<ValueClass>>, ValueClass>
rehashed on union.
notes:
Text of the former Manifest_ValueClass_Redesign.md "Out of scope for now" (e-graph), preserved here when the doc was rewritten normatively as doc/Optimization/Level_Two/Value_manifest.md (2026-11-11).  Note: congruence now merges through ValueState.usingClasses (mergeCongruentUsers), the nearest current analogue of the signature table described:

### Out of scope for now

`L2SemanticPrimitiveInvocation`. Its equivalences will eventually depend on
declared theorems with a representation/evaluation ranking (`a+a+a` to `a*3`
unless `b = a+a` is already computed; `{a,a,a} = {a}`; `|{a,a,a}| = 1`). That
work is e-graph saturation with a cost model for extraction, where
`ValueClass` is the e-class and `ValueState` is the e-class data, and it
needs a real signature table `Map<Pair<Primitive, List<ValueClass>>,
ValueClass>` rehashed on union. Steps 4 and 5 are the foundation it requires;
do not try to anticipate it further than that.
